blocks.html: On the macro front, data remained mixed. Solid US economic growth of 4.3% in the third quarter—its fastest pace in two years— was tempered by a softening US labor market which has seen unemployment creep higher and new job creation stall over the past few quarters. The Fed’s response clearly reflected these conflicting signals: The central bank delivered two rate cuts over the quarter and paused its balance sheet runoff but stopped short of an aggressive easing cycle as inflation remained above its 2% target. The AI narrative also evolved in important ways during the quarter. Momentum accelerated in October, reinforcing artificial intelligence as a key driver of capital investment and market performance. As the quarter progressed, investors questioned how much of the sector’s gains were already embedded in valuations, with several high-profile names trading at levels that were compared to periods of exuberance. Capital spending on data centers, semiconductors, and cloud infrastructure continued at a rapid pace, but limited visibility into near-term monetization raised concerns that investment intensity was running ahead of returns. The M&A market, in contrast, suffered no such ambiguity. The rebound in deal activity that began in the third quarter carried through year-end, marking a decisive return of M&A as financing conditions stabilized, and confidence improved. North American transaction volumes rose to $2.4 trillion in 2025, the highest level since 2021 and the second-highest year on record. The unevenness in the macro data and AI narrative was also evident in the credit markets. While the high yield and leveraged loan markets posted respectable returns throughout 2025, pockets of underperformance were evident. CCC-rated high yield underperformed the broader high yield market by 180 basis points and 200 basis points, in the fourth quarter and full year, respectively, as high interest rates, deteriorating credit metrics and continued liability management activity pressured lower-rated structures.

Additionally, we have begun to see value in the subprime auto sector where we have been able to source whole loan pools while utilizing attractive bank financing to create downside protected structures that provide incremental spread in an otherwise historically tight environment. We began to diversify the Fund’s commercial real estate exposure away from primarily CRE CLOs to also include direct CRE Loans where we are able to purchase the raw asset and finance the entire pool using attractive bank financing. Q4 2025 Deal Highlights5

blocks.html: During the quarter, Apollo led a large-scale asset-backed financing supporting the lease of advanced compute infrastructure for artificial intelligence applications. We were introduced to Valor through Apollo-managed Vehicles’ participation in xAI’s ~$5 billion debt financing in June, where we were a lead investor. During that process, xAI outlined plans for billions in additional financing to fund GPU purchases through a separate, dedicated vehicle that would sit outside of xAI’s capital structure. Valor’s approach represented a departure from prior AI infrastructure financings with its triple-net GPU lease structure in which xAI, rather than Valor, is required to secure power and operate the equipment during the lease term. This contrasts with recent neocloud financings, where lenders are exposed to execution risk by the borrower, who must meet stringent uptime requirements to avoid revenue credits and, in extreme cases, even lease termination. In addition to the GPU collateral, the Fund is expected to benefit from what we view as enhanced xAI counterparty risk through an xAI guarantee. We believe this distinction matters: It shifts risk away from servicing and execution toward asset value and counterparty quality—factors that in our view are more measurable and more appropriately priced in a credit instrument. The transaction consisted of a $3.5 billion first-lien unitranche facility provided to a special purpose vehicle sponsored by Valor Equity Partners, which financed a five-year lease of approximately 111,000 NVIDIA GPUs to a subsidiary of xAI. Given the rapid depreciation profile of advanced GPUs, the structure accelerates principal recovery, with roughly 80% of capital returned by the end of year three and no reliance on residual value to fully achieve contractual returns.

blocks.html: During the quarter, we continued to deploy capital into a residential land investment supporting US homebuilders. The team began investing in this sub-pillar in the third quarter and has deployed $600 million as of the end of Q4. Our focus is on financing the purchase and development of fully entitled land, which is then sold to builders over time as finished lots. Builders make an upfront, non-refundable deposit and pay monthly option fees, providing current income, while periodic lot sales return capital gradually as homes are built. Risk protection comes from direct ownership of the underlying land, contractual cash flows, and the ability to slow deployment or pursue alternative exits if market conditions change. With short to medium project timelines and capital returned progressively, the investment reflects our focus on conservative structures that pair contractual income with hard assets in a core housing segment.

What Clients Are Asking

blocks.html: Clients continue to ask how we are approaching AI infrastructure amid the rapid pace of investment and market attention. Our starting point is scale. We believe the build-out of data centers, compute, power, and related infrastructure is now one of the largest capital investment cycles in decades, with projected spending at $5 trillion over the next five years6. What began as a largely self-funded capex effort by a handful of hyperscalers has evolved into a market-wide financing event, with debt playing an increasingly central role across public and private credit markets. Debate around whether this pace of investment proves durable or excessive is likely to persist, but the magnitude of capital required is no longer in dispute (Exhibit 1).

blocks.html: This shift can create a meaningful opportunity for asset-backed finance. The capital required to support AI infrastructure increasingly exceeds the capacity or flexibility of traditional lenders and public markets, particularly at the asset and project level. As a result, structured, private financings have become a critical part of how AI infrastructure is funded—often outside public issuance statistics, but no less impactful for credit markets. In this environment, ABF is well positioned to provide capital against essential infrastructure assets, where underwriting is anchored in contracted cash flows, asset quality, and structural protections rather than long-term equity growth assumptions.

blocks.html: As capital intensity rises, access to financing—rather than innovation alone—is emerging as a key constraint on how quickly AI ambitions can be realized. Our focus is deliberately credit-oriented. AI infrastructure assets are capital intensive and subject to rapid technology obsolescence cycles, particularly for compute and cooling equipment, which can turn over far more quickly than typical financing tenors. We therefore emphasize structures that align asset lives with amortization, allocate refresh and upgrade risk appropriately, and limit reliance on single-tenant or long-dated assumptions. Power availability, interim generation, and execution risk are also central underwriting considerations as the pace of development accelerates.

blocks.html: While public discussion often focuses on the timing of further policy moves, the broader consensus remains that rates are likely to stay higher for longer. Even after the cuts delivered in 2025, policy rates remain in the 3.5%–3.75% range, with economists generally expecting only two additional cuts in 2026. From a portfolio perspective, the Fund’s floating-rate exposure is fully hedged, limiting sensitivity to near-term rate movements. The policy outlook has also been shaped by political developments, including President Donald Trump’s decision to nominate Kevin Warsh to replace Jerome Powell as Federal Reserve Chair. While Warsh has expressed alignment with the administration’s views on monetary policy and has advocated for significant changes at the Fed—including a smaller balance sheet and a rethinking of inflation frameworks and forecasting models—the implications for the future path of rates remain open for debate.

Outlook

blocks.html: We enter 2026 excited about the year ahead. The macro backdrop—declining rates, solid economic growth, fiscal stimulus—has become more favorable for risk assets, with AI-related investment expected to provide an additional tailwind to growth in the coming year. We also expect the policy outlook will influence the market environment in 2026. The US economic headline resilience has masked a notable divergence in macro conditions between low- and high-income consumers, contributing to the so-called K- shaped economy. That imbalance is now driving policy. As the 2026 midterms approach, President Trump has signaled a willingness to intervene more directly in sectors that impact affordability. Since the start of the year, those signals have taken concrete form across multiple fronts, including proposals to restrict institutional ownership of single-family homes, direct up to $200 billion of purchases in mortgage-backed securities to push mortgage rates lower, impose a one-year 10% cap on credit card interest rates, and limit the pass-through of utility inflation tied to rising power demand from AI data centers. Whether fully implemented or not, we believe the direction is clear: reduce pressure on household balance sheets and lower the all-in cost of living for consumers. Against this backdrop, we increasingly more opportunities in the following three areas.

blocks.html: Concerns about the US housing market have persisted over the past several years, driven by higher mortgage rates and affordability pressures. We believed then, and continue to believe now, that the underlying health of the housing market remains strong. Where stress has emerged, it has been largely confined to higher-risk segments, rather than signaling broad-based deterioration.

This imbalance is a result of several factors including league-level debt restrictions, conservative ownership cultures, and a legacy of equity-led financing that have led to over-equitized balance sheets. For ABF, we believe these characteristics—long-duration revenue streams (anchored in media contracts), strong asset coverage, and limited refinancing risk—align well with disciplined underwriting and structured downside protection. You can read more about this opportunity in our recent white paper The Financing Gap in Sports: Unlocking a $2.5 Trillion Opportunity.

blocks.html: As AI-driven data center development accelerates, the primary constraint is increasingly power, not compute. Reliable electricity has become a critical bottleneck, elevating power generation from a supporting input to a core piece of AI infrastructure. We believe this shift can create a compelling opportunity for asset-backed finance, as operators are willing to pay for certainty of supply and power assets generate essential, contract-backed cash flows. Financing power infrastructure—particularly distributed and backup generation—offers strong downside protection through hard assets and durable revenue streams. These assets are mission-critical to data center operations and benefit from sustained demand as power requirements continue to rise.

blocks.html: The Apollo Asset-Backed Finance Fund (“ABF” or the “Fund”) seeks to provide investors with a dedicated asset-backed finance offering in a semi-liquid and fully funded format. The Fund aims to generate consistent portfolio returns for investors across all economic cycles by investing in global asset- backed finance opportunities of various asset types, vintages, maturities, and capital structure priorities. The Fund seeks to identify investments in what Apollo believes are high-quality asset-backed products, focusing on large, diversified pools of hard assets and/or contracted cashflows, further enhanced by equity investments in Apollo origination platforms and targeting an overall net return of 10-14%10 with low correlation to traditional asset classes.

blocks.html: The Fund seeks to enhance portfolio construction using asset-level analysis and leveraging the Apollo platform’s structuring expertise. ABF invests across six key pillars: (1) consumer finance, (2) residential mortgage, (3) commercial mortgage, (4) hard assets, (5) financial assets and (6) capital solutions. The Fund maintains no bias to any of the six pillars and the objective of the Fund is to pursue what Apollo believes will be the highest risk/reward opportunities pursuant to a relative value framework.

GENERALLY, “MISREPRESENTATION” MEANS AN UNTRUE STATEMENT OF A MATERIAL FACT OR AN OMISSION TO STATE A MATERIAL FACT THAT IS REQUIRED TO BE STATED OR THAT IS NECESSARY TO MAKE A STATEMENT NOT MISLEADING IN LIGHT OF THE CIRCUMSTANCES IN WHICH IT WAS MADE. EACH PURCHASER SHOULD REFER TO PROVISIONS OF THE APPLICABLE SECURITIES LEGISLATION FOR THE PARTICULARS OF THESE RIGHTS OR CONSULT WITH A LEGAL ADVISOR. RIGHTS FOR PURCHASERS IN ONTARIO SECURITIES LEGISLATION IN ONTARIO PROVIDES, IN RELEVANT PART, THAT IF THE PRIVATE PLACEMENT MEMORANDUM, TOGETHER WITH ANY AMENDMENT THERETO, IS DELIVERED TO A PURCHASER OF INTERESTS RESIDENT IN ONTARIO BEFORE THE ISSUE OF SUCH INTERESTS TO SUCH PURCHASER AND CONTAINS A MISREPRESENTATION, SUCH PURCHASER WHO PURCHASES THE INTERESTS PURSUANT TO THE MEMORANDUM DURING THE PERIOD OF DISTRIBUTION SHALL BE DEEMED TO HAVE RELIED UPON THE MISREPRESENTATION IF IT WAS A MISREPRESENTATION AT THE TIME OF PURCHASE, AND SHALL, AS HEREINAFTER PROVIDED, HAVE A RIGHT OF ACTION AGAINST THE FUND FOR DAMAGES OR, ALTERNATIVELY, WHILE STILL THE OWNER OF THE PURCHASED INTERESTS, FOR RESCISSION, PROVIDED THAT NO ACTION SHALL BE COMMENCED TO ENFORCE THESE RIGHTS MORE THAN, (A) IN THE CASE OF AN ACTION FOR RESCISSION, 180 DAYS AFTER THE DATE OF THE TRANSACTION THAT GAVE RISE TO THE CAUSE OF ACTION; OR (B) IN THE CASE OF AN ACTION FOR DAMAGES, THE EARLIER OF: (I) 180 DAYS AFTER THE PURCHASER FIRST HAD KNOWLEDGE OF THE FACTS GIVING RISE TO THE CAUSE OF ACTION, OR (II) THREE YEARS AFTER THE DATE OF THE TRANSACTION THAT GAVE RISE TO THE CAUSE OF ACTION; PROVIDED, HOWEVER, AMONG OTHER THINGS: (A) NO PERSON OR COMPANY WILL BE LIABLE IF IT PROVES THAT THE PURCHASER PURCHASED THE INTERESTS WITH KNOWLEDGE OF THE MISREPRESENTATION, (B) IN THE CASE OF AN ACTION FOR DAMAGES, THE DEFENDANT WILL NOT BE LIABLE FOR ALL OR ANY PORTION OF THE DAMAGES THAT IT PROVES DO NOT REPRESENT THE DEPRECIATION IN VALUE OF THE INTERESTS AS A RESULT OF THE MISREPRESENTATION RELIED UPON; AND (C) IN NO CASE WILL THE AMOUNT RECOVERABLE IN ANY ACTION EXCEED THE PRICE AT WHICH THE INTERESTS WERE SOLD TO THE PURCHASER.
